entry.englishMeaning: to combine different elements smoothly into a whole
entry.coreIdea: Bring different elements together so they work smoothly as a whole.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract extension of mixing: combine different abilities or elements so they work together.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Usually constructive here because the combination is described as effective.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Explanatory, but the sentence is cut off, so the complete contrast between the abilities cannot be established.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and natural in creative, educational and professional discussion. Name the elements rather than leave the combination vague.

when_to_use: Describe combining ideas, styles or methods so that they work well together.
when_not_to_use: If you only put separate items in the same place, without combining them, use collect or group rather than blend.

advanced_nuance: Blend can describe ideas or styles without any physical mixing. It often presents their combination as smooth or harmonious, but does not prove the result is effective.
The saved source quotation is incomplete. It supports the combining sense but does not identify all the elements or the full argument.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: We blend theory to practice in this course.

entry.englishMeaning: to hold someone responsible for a fault or problem
entry.coreIdea: Say that someone is responsible for a problem or fault.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract verb for assigning responsibility for a fault; here, an entire team is held responsible to avoid confronting one individual.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Usually negative toward the person blamed; it may also imply an unfair accusation depending on the evidence.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Self-critical here: the writer presents indirect blame as a way people avoid a difficult individual conversation.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common everyday and professional vocabulary. “Identify responsibility” is more neutral when the aim is analysis rather than accusation.

when_to_use: Describe saying who is responsible for a mistake or an unwanted result.
Use do not blame someone when you reject an accusation or understand their reaction.
when_not_to_use: For positive results, use credit rather than blame: credit the team for its success.
When responsibility is uncertain, explain the evidence or say may have contributed instead of making an unsupported accusation.

advanced_nuance: Someone can blame a person unfairly: the verb reports an assignment of responsibility, not proof of guilt.
I do not blame you can express sympathy with a reaction, as in I do not blame you for feeling disappointed. The wording may reassure rather than accuse.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: An accusation points from a problem to someone held responsible.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Do not blame the whole team for one person’s mistake.
memory_practice.recall_question: Which preposition follows the person in blame someone ___ a mistake?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Compare They blame Mina for the error with They blame the error on Mina. Do they assign responsibility to the same person? Explain.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a fair response to someone who wants to blame an entire team before checking the facts. Use blame and name the problem.

examples.example_1: Do not blame the whole team for a mistake made by one person.
examples.example_2: They blame the delay on a missing part, but we still need to check what happened.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Do you blame Ravi for the missing file?
B: No. We do not yet know who moved it.
A: Then let us check the records first.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Afraid  to  confront  an  indi vidual,  we  blame  an  entire  team  for  a  problem-hoping  the  mess age  will  hit  the  right  target.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to hold someone responsible for a fault or problem
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writer describes holding a whole team responsible because someone is afraid to speak directly to one individual. Blaming the team does not prove that every member caused the problem.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: They blame the driver of the delay.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say They blame the driver for the delay, or They blame the delay on the driver.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Blame assigns responsibility for something bad. Criticize can express disapproval of someone’s work or behaviour without saying that they caused a particular problem.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: blame + person + for + problem/-ing; blame + problem + on + person/thing
common_collocations: blame the delay on bad weather

semanticReview.finding: Responsibility assignment distinguished from proven fault; both argument structures taught.

entry.englishMeaning: having named categories without an inherent order
entry.coreIdea: Label categories without ranking them from lower to higher.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Technical adjective for categories with names but no inherent ranking; job titles and countries illustrate labels rather than an ordered scale.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it describes a kind of variable, not the importance or quality of the categories.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Instructional here: the speaker gives examples to clarify the statistical sense.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Standard statistical and data-analysis terminology. This is not the everyday sense meaning very small or in name only.

when_to_use: Describe data categories such as blood groups or country names when the labels have no built-in ranking.
when_not_to_use: For ordered categories such as low, medium and high, use ordinal.
Do not use this statistical sense to explain a nominal fee, where nominal instead means very small.

advanced_nuance: The meaning of the recorded variable determines its scale. Displaying nominal labels alphabetically or assigning number codes does not create an inherent ranking.
Job titles are treated as labels in the source. If a study instead records ordered seniority levels, that is a different variable with an ordinal interpretation.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Name tags identify groups; they do not put the groups on a ladder.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Country names are nominal categories in this survey.
memory_practice.recall_question: Why does numbering nominal categories not turn them into measured quantities?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which is nominal: blood groups A/B/AB/O, or satisfaction levels low/medium/high? Explain whether the categories have an inherent order.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a sentence identifying one nominal variable in a survey and explain why its categories are not ranked.

examples.example_1: Blood group is a nominal variable because its categories do not form a ranking.
examples.example_2: The country labels in this survey are nominal categories, even if we display them alphabetically.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Are the country names ordinal or nominal data?
B: Nominal. One country label is not a higher rank than another.
A: So putting the names in alphabetical order does not create a ranking.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: That's useful when your categories are nominal, like job titles or countries.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: having named categories without an inherent order
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker describes categories treated as names or labels, without a built-in ranking. Countries are an example. Job titles can be treated as nominal labels here, although a particular organisation might also group roles by seniority.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: Assigning codes 1, 2 and 3 to nominal categories makes category 3 three times category 1.
mistakes_differences.correction: The codes are labels. They do not create numerical size, distance or rank between nominal categories.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Nominal categories distinguish types without a built-in order. Ordinal categories, such as low, medium and high, have an order, though their gaps need not be equal.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: nominal + data/variable/category/scale; the categories are + nominal

semanticReview.finding: Nominal versus ordinal distinction checked against NIST; number labels and job-title caveat treated accurately.
